title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The Companies That Spent Most Aggressively on AI in H1 Are Discounted First
dek: Capital markets can only rise if new money keeps buying in. Global liquidity is showing signs of peaking, and the companies that were most aggressive on AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.
who: For investors watching both US AI stocks and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary-market practitioners gauging the sources and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: The case-by-case discussion of Hong Kong IPOs can be skipped; the main thread starts at 8:11 with Nvidia's liquidity experiment.

points.h: A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
points.body: Do not read Hong Kong's low first-day break rate as a sign of a strengthening market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level normal under a market-based mechanism, meaning the main participants in IPOs are short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of listed companies has shrunk, and IPO-related funds have blown up, yet the two newly listed companies still broke issue, showing that temporary supply-side control has not solved the fundamental problem: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive on AI, the sooner punished
points.body: Market attitude reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were disclosed in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capex in the first half, especially those that spent all their free cash flow, was discounted — even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the whole supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before price hikes, and inventories still propping up gross margins. By Q3, inventories are depleted and the impact of price hikes returns, so the negatives will show up together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out rent-to-own to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as current sales. Nvidia is now also pushing rent-to-own. In its financials, free cash flow halved quarter-on-quarter, and receivables on the books are far above historical levels — speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure from rent-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached the stage where it needs more aggressive financial tactics to sustain capital-market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary-market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in the timing of fund fundraising. The money concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022; they barely deployed in 2023-2025, until they saw state capital betting and making the most money when no one dared to invest — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models, and two large chips stimulated market-based capital. The mentality is: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: The new property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key to recent real estate policy is not bailing out developers, but pulling households out of the old financing loop. In the past, buying pre-sale housing meant households played the role of financing targets in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers get completed homes and only bear the consumer role, with risk reset back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from breaking the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining industry consolidation followed similar paths.

points.h: A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
points.body: A slow bull does not rely on slogans, but on layering market chips by duration: the bottom layer is low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips taken up by insurance as long money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, playing a quasi-stabilizing role; Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjust the index at a higher layer; the top layer is retail, private funds, and active managers. The new insurance rules require liabilities and assets to match in term, yield, and liquidity, effectively ensuring long money for long investments, medium money for medium, and short money for short — not allowing short-term public money to be invested in ten-year low-liquidity assets.

points.h: Crises are rescued ever bigger, bubbles at least one and a half
points.body: After the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises by printing money, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared in a rate-hike cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then the pandemic hit in 2020, so a larger flood of money was layered on top of the previous bubble before it had dissipated — today at least one and a half bubbles have accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis appears, with the endogenous result that inflation, financial asset inflation, and wealth inequality intensify simultaneously. As long as bubbles are not allowed to clear, the world may face long-term stagflation in some form.

quotes.text: The reason I say it feels a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a bit of a problem with liquidity peaking.
In the capital market, whoever spends aggressively is seen as impressive, and then when half-year reports come out, it becomes whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where it needs rent-to-own to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone looks and says, if you can pull off this story like that, then I can certainly pull off this story like that too — psychologically it's roughly like that.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently slow and bullish; it has to first build a chip structure on top of the slow bull.
When the bubble piled up last time had not yet dissipated, a bigger one was added — and added without hesitation.
